report:
Conclusion: your skepticism is understandable, but for **adult out-of-hospital cardiac arrest (OHCA)** the claim is broadly supported: bystander hands-only/compression-only CPR is associated with better survival than **no bystander CPR**. The strongest direct statement comes from a JAMA study: “layperson compression-only CPR was associated with increased survival compared with conventional CPR and no bystander CPR” (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/186668). AHA guidance similarly frames Hands-Only CPR as a way to increase bystander action and improve survival (https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.110.970889), and an AHA science advisory states compression-only bystander CPR “substantially improves survival” versus no bystander CPR (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7746055/).

Important caveats: much of the “versus no CPR” evidence is observational, so it shows association rather than perfect causal proof; randomized trials mainly compared compression-only with conventional CPR, not with doing nothing. Recent work still finds CPR for OHCA is associated with higher survival, while the exact effect of very delayed bystander CPR is less certain (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0300957225000784). Exceptions matter: children and likely respiratory/asphyxial arrests generally need conventional CPR with breaths when possible. Overall, the evidence does not support calling the adult claim false.
